newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil current account gap "healthy" - cenbank.
newsitem.headline: Brazil current account gap "healthy" - cenbank.

text.p: Brazil's current account gap, which reached 2.89 percent of gross domestic product in the first 10 months of 1996, is healthy because it is being financed by higher-quality capital, a Central Bank official said.
Altamir Lopes, head of the bank's economics department, said 38.5 percent of the January-October deficit was financed by $6.638 billion of foreign direct investment (FDI).
The bank expects FDI to finance 40 percent of the expected year-end current account deficit of 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, he said.
"We have a slight increase in the current account deficit from September to October but we also have resources of better quality to finance the deficit," Lopes told reporters.
Lopes, comparing Brazil's external accounts now with the period after last year's Mexico peso crisis, said the situation was fundamentally much healthier.
Brazil's current account gap in January to October 1995 represented 2.7 percent of GDP compared with 2.89 percent in the same period this year.
But FDI covered only 22.1 percent of the deficit in the whole of 1995, the Central Bank said.

"We lost $7.0 billion in reserves due to the Tequila effect (of the recent Mexican peso crisis)," Lopes said. "If it happened again, the impact would be much less because we are financing the (current account) gap less with short-term capital."
In terms of Brazilian overseas issues, maturities and conditions had also improved "significantly" in October over the third quarter of 1996, Lopes said.
Of all placements, including both private and public sector, average maturities for Brazilian paper abroad rose to 7.4 years in October from an average of 7.2 years in he third quarter.
Spreads also narrowed to an average of 379 basis points over U.S. Treasury Notes from 465 basis points (bp), Lopes said.
The gains were led by the public sector, with three issues in October, including a $750 million global bond, enjoying an average maturity of 6.8 years and spread of 307 bp.
There were no public sector issues in the third quarter but in the second quarter, Brazilian government paper paid 374 bp and had an average maturity of 4.4 years.
"I cannot remember the last time, it was so long ago, that Brazilian debt paid a spread as low as 307 bp," Lopes said.
